title: KV reuse: IO slip and reuse-entropy sprint log
content:
Sprint log: KV reuse entropy + IO-slip investigations

Summary:
- Goal: understand repeated small-window cache misses that produce repeated NVMe reads (we call these IO-slips) and their connection to apparent reuse-entropy spikes in multi-tenant workloads.
- Hypothesis: skewed micro-hotspots with intermittent sequence-length changes cause eviction cascades across memory banks, producing short bursts of NVMe read amplification and elevated per-token tail latency.

Why this matters:
- Host throughput drops ~8-12% during 99th percentile tail events; billing and SLA risk for Dedicated nodes.
- Prefetching tuned for average reuse worsened read amplification when hotset footprint oscillates.

Environment / setup:
- Hardware: 8x A800 GPUs (64GB), 2x PCIe 4 NVMe per host, 6-channel DRAM per CPU socket, kernel 5.15 tune.
- Runtime: serving v0.67.3 (kv allocator: slab-v2), prefetcher = credit-based 64-window, eviction = combined-LRU+age heuristic.
- Workloads: mix of chat (seqlen 64-512) + embeddings bursts (seqlen 16) + scheduled ranking jobs (seqlen 128).
- Synthetic probe: hotkey blast generator (zipfian skews 0.6/0.9) overlayed with 10% high-seqlen tails.

Observations (field runs + synthetic):
1) IO-slip signature:
   - Short bursts (200-800ms) of NVMe reads where a set of ~1.2-2.4M KV pages are read repeatedly across multiple requests.
   - Read amplification factor (measured bytes read / unique bytes requested) spikes to 3.2x during slips.
   - Prefetch queue occupancy drops to zero for ~100-300ms then floods, correlating with eviction churn.

2) Reuse-entropy behavior:
   - Distribution: median reuse rate ~18%, long tail with 95th at 62% depending on tenant mix.
   - Entropy metric (Shannon across sampled key-residence histograms) increases by 25-40% preceding slips.
   - Correlated with sequence-length shifts: when a tenant switches from short to long context, KV access patterns spread and previously pinned pages are evicted.

3) Bank/channel hotspots & eviction cascades:
   - Hotset concentrated on 1-2 memory channels (measured by channel-local page fetch counts). When hotset migrates, bank-local bandwidth saturates; DMA queue latency climbs 2.5x.
   - Eviction waves originate from channels with highest occupancy; cross-channel balancing is delayed due to allocator's zone affinity.

4) Latencies & tail impact:
   - Per-token P50 unaffected; P95 increases by 18-30% and P99 by 40-70% during slips.
   - End-to-end request P99 for chat workloads jumps from 320ms -> 540ms in worst runs.

Benchmarks / micro-probes run:
- Trace replay (10M requests): baseline prefetch-credit=64 -> measured read amplification 1.15x, reuse 21%.
- Adjusted prefetch-credit=16 (more conservative): reuse stable but P99 down by 9% during slip windows, read amplification reduced to 1.05x.
- Aggressive pinning (pin top-8% resident keys): reduces slip frequency by ~45% but increases steady-state memory occupancy and reduces headroom for bursts.

Quick root-cause sketch:
- The allocator's zone affinity + credit-based prefetcher tuned on mean seqlen leads to over-prefetching of now-stale pages while evictor removes active pages from congested channels, causing repeat reads when access distribution shifts.

Mitigations tried (results):
- Staggered-prefetch-slew: add randomized backoff to prefetch triggers per-tenant -> slip frequency down 30%, minimal cost to throughput.
- Channel-aware eviction: prototype that rebalances eviction targets across channels -> reduces DMA latency spikes by ~22% but increases metadata overhead.
- Short-term pin windows: pin hot keys for 250ms after first hit -> effective for very-high-skew tenants but harms multi-tenant fairness.

New proposal (next sprint):
1) Adaptive-prepass: on seqlen-class shift detect, throttle prefetch credits for 400ms and opportunistically refresh KV pins only for keys with strong reuse signatures (LRU delta + recent access slope).
2) Channel-fair reclamation: soft-migrate low-reuse pages across channels during idle windows to reduce future bank hotspots.
3) IO-slip detector: lightweight anomaly detector (exponentially-weighted moving reuse entropy + prefetch drain rate) to trigger emergency backoffs and temporary pin policies.

Telemetry / instrumentation additions needed:
- Per-channel KV-access histograms sampled at 100ms granularity.
- Read-amplification counter split by tenant and seq-length class.
- Prefetch queue drain-time tracing and correlation with eviction events.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Long-term effects of soft-migration on NVMe wear and billing costs (need cost sim).
- Are there workload signals we can expose to customers so they can avoid patterns (e.g., staging sudden seqlen jumps)?
- Edge cases with on-prem networks where NVMe latency variance is larger than cloud baseline.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Proto adaptive-prepass: Ethan Shaw (spike + bench) due 2026-03-08.
- Telemetry PR: Priya Nair (add per-channel histograms) due 2026-02-26.
- Run extended A/B on dedicated pool (20 hosts) with channel-aware eviction: Maya Hernandez + SRE, 2-week run starting 2026-03-02.

Notes to self / rough commands:
- replay tool: ./bench/replay --trace=prod-feb --rate=12k --seqlen-dist=hybrid --sample-hotkeys=0.1
- collect: sudo perf record -e nvme:* -a sleep 60; ./scripts/parse-nvme-perf.py
- quick check: curl -sS localhost:8080/_telemetry?sample=channel_hist | jq .top_channels

References / context links:
- JIRA-ENG-3421: prefetch credit tuning followup
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-prefetch/pull/87 (staggered backoff prototype)

Closing: this is still a messy set of signals but consistent enough to justify the adaptive prepass + channel rebalancer approach. We should prioritize lightweight telemetry first so we can measure the effectiveness of mitigation in production without a full rollout.

-- Maya
